doc.title: Harry Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 13, 1997

title: Where jazz is headed and building an audience
summary: Hopes to be in the middle of it; Iowa lighting engineer anecdote shows new listeners respond; need for publicity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: So you’re thirty now, let’s see, you’ll be a veteran jazz musician in your seventies when it’s two thousand— I can’t do this math. I’m just wondering, where is jazz going to be in thirty years. Because when you look at the history of jazz it’s moved so fast. Sometimes I feel it moves too fast for its own good you know. Like Miles never seemed to be happy with what he was doing and the audience would just catch up with him and then he’d be somewhere else.
Well it’s hard to say what’s going to happen with jazz, but whatever happens, I just hope I’m in the middle of it. That’s the main thing.
Do you anticipate that you’re going to be able to make a living in this music? You don’t see why not.

Yeah. I’ve had a lot of experiences that give me hope, and here’s one of them. I was playing at a college somewhere in Iowa in a small — I forget the name of the town. But there was a college in Iowa and they had a light engineer that was there that the only reason he was there was he had done the lighting for the rock & roll show the night before. And they said oh just leave the stuff and do the jazz concert. And he heard us at the jazz concert and he came up to us afterwards and said, “Wow, that’s the most beautiful music I’ve ever heard.” He’d never heard it. Once he did hear it, he loved it. And I think a lot of people are like that and the press has weird notions of what is jazz and what isn’t jazz, and a lot of people when they hear jazz like this, who swear that they don’t like jazz, like this. So I’m confident that there will always be an audience for it. It’s up to us to promote it in such a way that the audience knows about it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Yeah. We need more audience. I don’t know if we need a lot more players. I’m concerned sometimes about the amount of players that are coming out of music colleges and where are they all going to go? We need to get more audience to go with it I guess.

It’s all just the publicity thing. If we can get the right publicity and pick the right — you know if the music industry went on a quality basis and promoted it right, I don’t think there would be a problem getting the audience.
